newsitem.title: CONGO: Congo rivals extend truce as French troops quit.
newsitem.headline: Congo rivals extend truce as French troops quit.

text.p: Congo's warring factions agreed on Friday to extend their truce for a further week, just hours after France pulled the last of its soldiers out of the capital Brazzaville.
"The chiefs of staff (of both sides) have agreed to prolong the ceasefire for a period of seven days starting tonight (Friday) at midnight (2300 GMT)," they said in a joint statement.
It was read to Reuters by a spokesman for Bernard Kolelas, the city's mayor who has been mediating between President Pascal Lissouba and his rival and predecessor, Denis Sassou Nguesso.
Fighting between the two men's forces flared in the capital on June 5, killing hundreds of people and prompting France to mount a major military operation to evacuate foreigners.
Ignoring calls for them to stay from a U.N. special envoy, the 1,250 French troops completed their pullout on Friday, leaving the warring sides to their own devices.

"The last soldiers left today," ambassador Raymond Cesaire, the one remaining Western envoy, told Reuters by telephone. "That leaves 30 gendarmes who are staying to protect the diplomats, that is myself and 12 colleagues."

The atmosphere earlier on Friday at Brazzaville airport, which was the French base and a key target for the fighters, was not one of confidence in the chances of a lasting peace, but rather of people abandoning a sinking ship.

Scores of Malians trapped there for days were picked up by a charter flight, while many Mauritanians waited for someone to take them away. Airlines stripped their hangars and offices of all they could, and flew their planes away.

Earlier, an international Red Cross team took 60 children from an orphanage in the no man's land around the airport to safety in Bacongo, a southern suburb held by Kolelas' neutral militia to which thousands of residents have fled.
The ceasefire, which began on Wednesday, held firm on Friday, giving people courage to venture gingerly out into the streets, amid rotting bodies and shops looted clean.

The extension of the truce -- accompanied by a pledge by both sides to crack down on "wrongdoers, looters and killers" was a positive sign amid widespread fears that fighting could resume after the French departure.

U.N. envoy Mohamed Sahnoun, who with African mediators has called on the Security Council to send an African intervention force to "Brazza", repeatedly urged Paris to keep at least some troops in position until such a force arrived.

Despite the withdrawal, Paris has not ruled out playing a future role in peace efforts in its old colony. Foreign Minister Hubert Vedrine will discuss this on Monday with U.N. Secretary- General Kofi Annan, a ministry spokesman said.

After losing face in Africa by backing Zaire's hated president Mobutu Sese Seko, ousted last month by rebel leader Laurent Kabila, France has taken a less confident line in its dealings with its former colonies, analysts say.

There are some 8,000 French troops based in former African colonies where they have intervened at least 15 times in internal conflicts. One French soldier was killed in the Brazzaville operation, which was purely an evacuation.
Congo's trouble began when Lissouba, a friend of Mobutu's, tried to disarm the militia of Marxist-turned-capitalist Sassou Nguesso, whom he had succeeded as president in 1992 elections.
The foes were, along with Kolelas, front-runners in presidential elections due in late July and now postponed.
The European Union appealed for both sides to put the democratic process back on track, French radio reported.
